label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**Why I'm keeping the busing project (or: a long reply to a short text)**

Jess texted me last night: "it's one assignment, don't torch your job over it." Half the group chat hearted it, and a couple of you added your own versions. I started typing a reply, deleted it, started again, and realized I was about to send fifteen texts that would each make about a third of a point. So I'm doing it here, once.

This is for all of you, but mostly it's for Jess. Jess, I'm not mad. I know exactly why you said it, and I'd probably say the same thing to you. I'm not trying to win this. I just want you to understand why I'm doing what I'm doing, even if you still think I'm being an idiot afterward.

**The project, for anyone who hasn't heard me talk about it**

I teach two sections of US History II, all juniors. Every fall for the last four years at Cobb Street, I've given them the same assignment: find someone in your family or your neighborhood who lived through the 1974–76 busing crisis in Boston, interview them, and turn in a ten-minute recording and a two-page reflection.

That's it. Four years, no complaints. Then a couple of weeks ago a parent emailed my principal and cc'd someone on the school committee. She wrote that the project "reopens wounds" and "pressures kids to judge their grandparents." My principal would like me to quietly let it go. There's a meeting next Thursday, the 19th, at 3:15, with the three of us.

I'm not going to drop it. I'm going to change it, though, and I'll get to that.

**The part where Jess is right**

I want to say this before anything else so nobody thinks I'm pretending: yes, I could get burned. I've been tenured since 2021, so nobody's firing me over an oral history assignment. But tenure doesn't protect you from everything. My principal decides my schedule, and my principal decides who teaches AP. There are a lot of quiet ways to make a teacher's year worse, and none of them leave a paper trail. Jess has spent the last several years in HR. She knows how institutions handle people who are a pain, and she's not wrong about it.

I'm also a little scared. I'd love to tell you I'm calm and principled about this, but mostly I've been lying awake running through the meeting in my head and coming up with better answers at 2 a.m. I don't feel brave. I just keep landing in the same place.

**The part where the parent is right**

This might surprise some of you: I think she has a point.

The way I've run the project, the default is to interview your own family. For most kids that's great. Some families, though, have a grandfather who was on the wrong side of a police line in 1974, or an aunt who still won't talk about it, or relationships that are already fragile. When I tell a sixteen-year-old "go ask Grandma about busing," I'm putting something on that kid that I don't fully see. I've always told them they could come talk to me if it was a problem, but sixteen-year-olds mostly don't do that. They just do the thing, or they don't, and either way they've been carrying something by themselves.

So the pressure is real. I'd been treating "you can always come to me" as if it were the same thing as a real choice, and it isn't.

**What I'm actually proposing**

I'm keeping the project, and I'm adding a second path that's just as legitimate as the first. Kids can interview a librarian or an archivist about the busing records, or they can work with the recorded interviews from past years. We have four years of them now, and I'd only use the ones where students and their families give permission. Nobody will have to interview family, and nobody will have to explain why they picked the other option. I'll grade both the same way.

The line for me is simple: I don't get to force anyone. I do get to keep offering it.

**Why I won't just drop it**

I keep thinking of two kids.

In 2023, a boy I'll call D. interviewed his grandmother. It turned out she'd driven a school bus in South Boston in 1974. Nobody in the family knew. She had never told her own kids. D. asked if he could play part of the recording for the class, and he played maybe forty seconds of her describing the morning. When it ended, the room was silent for what felt like a full minute. Juniors, quiet for a minute, without me asking. I've been teaching for over a decade and I can count those moments on one hand.

Last year a girl found out from her interview that her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was really upset. We talked after class twice, and I was honestly not sure I'd done the right thing by assigning it. Then she turned in her reflection. It was the best piece of writing I read all year, and I'm including the stuff I read for fun. She didn't excuse her uncle and she didn't write him off. She tried to hold both things, the person she knows and the thing he did, which is exactly what we want people to be able to do with history and almost never manage.

That's the part I can't get past. The kids who are uncomfortable with this are often the ones who need it most. I know how that sounds. It sounds like "it's good for you," which is what people say right before doing something to you that isn't. That's exactly why the alternate option matters so much to me. If a kid needs to step back, they can. But I don't want to make the whole subject vanish because it's hard for some families. The hardness is kind of the point.

And this is their city. These kids get off the T at the same stops. Some of them live on streets that were in the news in 1974. The textbook gives the whole thing one paragraph. One. If I drop the project, that paragraph is what they get, and the next time a version of this argument comes up in Boston, and it will, they'll have nothing to connect it to.

**What I'm not doing**

I'm not picking a fight with this parent. I don't think she's a villain and I don't plan to walk into that meeting treating her like one. My guess is she's protecting her kid, or her family, or maybe herself, and I understand all three. I'd honestly like to hear more from her about what happened at home, because if the project went badly for her family, I want to know how, so I can do it better.

I'm also not trying to turn this into a free speech crusade or a big story. I don't want it on anyone's Facebook. I want to teach a good unit and keep teaching it.

**Jess**

You and I met student teaching in 2012, in that building with the radiators that clanged all of third period. You were the better teacher that year and we both know it. When you left in 2019 I was sad, and I also understood completely. You'd given it everything and it wasn't giving much back. I think part of your text was about that. You've seen what this job does to people who keep pushing, and you don't want to watch it happen to me.

I love that you're looking out for me, and I mean that. I'm not asking you to agree. I'm asking you to know that I thought about it, that I'm not being reckless, and that I'm compromising where I think the parent has a point. I just can't make myself treat this as "one assignment." For a few kids every year it's the most real thing that happens in my classroom, and I'm not ready to stop doing that because it got hard.

The meeting's Thursday at 3:15. I'll text you after, probably from my car in the parking lot, probably something incoherent. Answer it anyway. If it goes badly you get to say you told me so, once, and then you have to buy me a drink.

---

A couple of notes: I used "my principal" instead of Dr. Halvorsen's name, since the post is public-ish and the meeting hasn't happened yet. It's easy to put back if you want it. I also kept the students down to D. and "a girl," with no names or identifying details. It's about 1,350 words.
